Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: rehearse what to say before any interaction

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

vignette: Seventy‑seven‑year‑old Maru, a Pacific Islander interior designer who once painted rooms for diplomatic officials, sat in his modest studio surrounded by unfinished canvases and the faint scent of linseed oil when he finally decided to reach out for help. Maru’s life had been punctuated by the memory of a four‑week captivity he endured during a 1999 deployment in the South Pacific. In a cramped, stone cell with only a single barred window, he was surrounded by the guttural shouting of captors speaking Arabic, the metallic clink of chains, and the oppressive weight of their threats. He could still feel the chill of the stone walls and hear the echo of each command. Those images and sounds had become more than memories; they had become triggers that could arrive without warning, flaring up from the back of his mind like a sudden flash. The day he had been captured, Maru’s mind would sometimes erupt in an intrusive memory that felt almost like a film running in real time. A sudden surge of auditory recollection—a shiver-inducing shout in Arabic—would jolt him into a state where he felt utterly emotionally vulnerable. In the span of seconds he would find himself rehearsing the next conversation he would have to make, as if rehearsing a script could protect him from the threat of being spoken to again. The mere thought of entering a confined office space made his chest tighten; he would find himself steering clear of enclosed rooms, insisting on a desk by a window, always ensuring his back was against a wall where he could see the whole room. Those avoidance habits were Maru’s attempt to control the unpredictable. When Maru’s mind slipped back into that captured cell, the threat that rose from the remembered fear was immediate. He would feel a surge of negative emotions—fear, horror, anger, guilt—before he could even name them. His body would react before his thoughts could: a racing heart, the urge to clutch his chest, the sudden need to look toward a wall for protection. The experience was so intense that sometimes his recall became emotionless, a detached recording of the event, or so fragmented that he could not explain the story clearly without losing the thread. Yet, oddly, the memory would still echo with the harsh voices from his captivity, and his mind would replay those sounds as if they were new. The cycle of threat, memory, and trigger was a loop. The fear and negative emotions that burst forth would often send a new intrusive memory racing into Maru’s mind. That intrusiveness, in turn, would be the trigger that led him back into the same defensive behaviors—rehearsing conversations, avoiding confined workspaces, and refusing to return to the studio where he once found creative freedom. His rehearsals, which were meant to stave off threat, instead reinforced the memory, turning an emotionless recall into a living echo. The rehearsed words and the avoidance behaviors both served to maintain the threat, keeping his body in a constant state of readiness. Maru’s avoidance of his studio had tangible consequences. His clients had begun to notice the delay in his responses; projects stalled, and a steady stream of commissions dwindled. The interior design firm he had worked with for over a decade began to look for replacements, citing his lack of presence and the perceived unreliability. The loss of his work was not just professional—it was a personal blow that further amplified his sense of failure and guilt, which he believed had arisen from his failure to protect himself during his captivity. He started to avoid not only the physical spaces associated with work but also the very idea of study or learning new design trends. Even simple tasks, such as reviewing a new color palette, would set off the same chain of intrusive memory, threat, and avoidance. Now, at the age of sixty‑seven, Maru’s interior design studio sits half‑empty, the walls echoing with the silence of unfinished projects. The day he finally sought help was a quiet afternoon when he found himself staring at a color swatch for the hundredth time, unable to commit to a choice because his body was already tense and his mind was replaying the Arabic shout from his cell. He feared that stepping back into the studio would trigger the memory again, and he was terrified of the negative emotions that would follow. Yet he also hoped that confronting this cycle would allow him to reclaim the space he once filled with creativity and not feel as if his past had hijacked his present. Maru’s main fear is that the threat will never abate, that his body will continue to react before he can think, and that he will forever be living in a state of perpetual vigilance. He seeks relief, hoping that through therapy he can break the loop that binds his memory, threat, and avoidance into a relentless spiral.
